(1) How to Distinguish Legislative Rules from Interpretive 
Rules and General Statements of Policy
Interpretive rules® and general statements of policy (a.k.a. policy 
statements) are known collectively as guidance J Guidance can encompass 
any agency statement that is applicable to a generic class of persons and 
describes how an agency interprets law or exercises discretion. Given that 
statutes and legislative rules can never resolve all the questions that arise 
in operating a complex administrative scheme, guidance—and lots of it— 
is a necessity for an agency that wishes to control its field personnel and 
keep the public informed about how to comply with the agency’s program. 
Hence, the volume of guidance “greatly exceeds that of notice-and-comment 
regulation. Peter L. Strauss, Publication Pules in the Rulemaking 
Spectrum: Assuring Proper Respect for an Essential Element, 53 Ad min . L. 
Re v . 803, 804—05 (2001). Examples of guidance include announcements by 
the agency of its strategy for handling some upcoming problem (sometimes 
labeled “order,” “notice,” “memorandum,” etc.); manuals for agency staff on 
how to implement statutes and legislative rules; and manuals for 
stakeholders on what they can expect of the agency and how best to comply 
with the agency’s thinking. Often this last type of manual is composed of 
answers that staff draw up to coordinate their responses to “frequently 
asked questions” from stakeholders, e.g., regulated companies phoning or 
e-mailing to ask, “If we do ABC, does that constitute MNO under the XYZ 
Act?” Guidance can also include even less formal utterances, such as letters 
in response to queries from regulated parties, beneficiaries, or members of 
Congress. Thousands of queries flowed in to the Cost of Living Council 
under the Wage Stabilization Act discussed in Chapter 2. Indeed, 
answering such questions is one of the major activities of agencies like the 
Internal Revenue Service. Sh a l in i Bh a r g a v a Ra y , INDIVIDUALIZED
